title: Outcomes of pharmacist-led support for voluntary opioid tapering in a multidisciplinary pain clinic: a prospective observational study
abstract: Objective: to describe dose, pain interference, withdrawal, disengagement and acute harm over 12 months among adults entering a pharmacist-led opioid tapering pathway. Design: prospective observational study of consecutive entries from November 2026 to October 2027. Setting: multidisciplinary pain clinic of a regional hospital. Participants: about 85 adults on 50 mg oral morphine equivalents a day or more who chose to taper. Main outcome: percent change in daily dose at 6 months from dispensing data. Results and conclusions will be written when 12-month data exist.
introduction: Supported tapering of long-term opioids is widely recommended, but most reports are uncontrolled, define success by different dose thresholds and rarely follow patients who stop attending. Fast reductions carry a short-term excess of overdose and withdrawal-related emergency visits, so safety outcomes matter as much as dose. This study describes outcomes for every patient entering one pharmacist-led pathway, including those who disengage.
methods: Consecutive adults entering the pathway over 12 months are followed for 12 months each, with outcomes collected at the existing fortnightly pharmacist calls and at 6 and 12 month clinic visits. Dose comes from the dispensing history, which remains available after disengagement for participants who consented at entry. Pain interference is rated from 0 to 10 and withdrawal with an eight-item telephone checklist. Disengagement is defined as no contact for six weeks and modelled on two pre-specified predictors, distance over 60 km and interpreter need.
results: No data have been collected yet. The report will give the mean percent change in dose with its interval, the course of pain interference, withdrawal scores around dose steps, emergency visits and overdose for all participants, and disengagement by distance and interpreter need.
discussion: The discussion will set the observed dose change against the two-clinic follow-up and the before-after report, noting that the latter's headline figure was corrected after publication. It will not attribute change to the pathway, because there is no concurrent comparison.
limitations: There is no comparison group, participants chose to taper, and all data come from one clinic. Pain interference is self-reported and missing for patients who leave, although dose and emergency visits are not.
conclusion: To be written after 12-month follow-up of the last participant. It will describe outcomes of pathway patients and will not claim that the pathway caused them.
summary: STROBE-structured draft with results left empty until data exist.
